A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same coalition-attribution framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v2 presents mathematical results, proofs and illustrative examples. Figure 1 is a conceptual illustration; neither the main text nor Appendices A–B report original empirical outcomes.

after.justification: v3 reports original numerical verification, synthetic-function experiments, NLP and image evaluations, and Go analyses involving five experts. Results appear in Tables 2–5 and Figures 2–7, including Appendices I–J.

M1.justification: The coalition-attribution formula in Equation (6) and sparse AND-OR extraction remain unchanged. v3 adds derived faithfulness scores R, R' and Q, plus selection of Go coalition candidates using top-ranked interaction strengths alongside manual annotation. These extend the framework without redesigning its attribution calculation.

E1.justification: v2 has no empirical dataset or task coverage. v3 evaluates synthetic-function regression, SST-2 sentiment classification, MNIST and CIFAR-10 image classification, and KataGo shape-pattern explanations, including expert assessments. The NLP and image examples in v2 were illustrative rather than evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical comparisons against competing attribution algorithms. v3's Table 1 conceptually compares Shapley, Banzhaf, Joint Shapley and Faith-Shap; these are not benchmarked baselines. Direct Shapley calculations in Table 2 serve as references for checking a mathematical identity.

E3.justification: v3 introduces experimental protocols absent from v2: reconstruction checks across coalition sizes 1–10, three faithfulness metrics, MLP regression on 20 target functions, and meaningful-versus-random coalition controls. Further settings include BERT-large/LLaMA fine-tuning, ten selected input variables, and Go analyses after 40 moves. These are new experiments, not revisions of established v2 protocols.

E4.justification: v3 adds numerical checks of the attribution and output decompositions, controlled tests distinguishing faithful, partially faithful and unfaithful synthetic coalitions, and semantic coalition case studies. Appendix J adds expert analysis of Go patterns and how adding particular stones changes their attribution. v2 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3 introduces averaged point estimates and individual examples, but no uncertainty-estimation practice; the five Go experts are participants, not repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds all empirical result entries. Table 2 reports Shapley reconstruction errors from 3.6×10^-8 to 9.1×10^-7; Table 4 reports mean Q values of 0.948, 0.590 and 0.013 for faithful, partially faithful and unfaithful coalitions. Tables 3 and 5 and Figures 2–7 add further reconstruction, NLP, image and Go findings. There are no corresponding v2 measurements for performance-change comparisons.

T1.justification: The principal decomposition results are retained under new numbering. v3 adds anonymity and coalition-level symmetry axioms, strengthens the dummy condition from all coalition members being dummy to at least one, and formally defines three faithfulness measures. Appendices E–G supply additional proofs for decompositions, axioms and efficiency; v2's universal-matching equation is relocated, not newly introduced.

C1.justification: v3 retains the coalition-attribution and conflict-mechanism claims but expands the central contribution to evaluating whether grouped variables form faithful coalitions. Its abstract and introduction newly claim validation across synthetic, NLP, image and Go settings, consistency with human intuition, and practical value for Go players. v2 makes no comparable empirical or coalition-evaluation claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting faithfulness scores to coherent semantic units and low-scoring NLP groups to representation flaws. It acknowledges that learned interactions can differ from intended ones and that interaction computation restricts Go analysis to small subsets. Appendix J discusses disagreement with experts and hypothesizes a distinction between human tactical reasoning and the network's longer-term statistical patterns.

D1.justification: v3 adds limited reproducibility details for its experiments, including synthetic-function construction, 8×8 image partitioning, input-selection rules, and Go stone-removal, fixed-background and adjusted-output conventions. It does not provide full training hyperparameters, hardware/runtime information or code-release instructions for the proposed method.

R1.justification: v3 adds a substantial related-work section, Table 1 and Appendix A distinguishing coalition attribution from interaction effects. New discussion covers Joint Shapley, Faith-Shap, Shapley-Taylor, Archipelago and other approaches, positioning the paper's mathematical explanation of conflict against previous engineering treatments. v2 provides much narrower background and positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and retained theoretical material is reorganized into separate attribution, conflict-explanation and axioms subsections. v3 adds a dedicated related-work section and conclusion, restructures the appendices, and expands conceptual explanations. The author list also removes Bo Fan.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from one column to two and redraws and relocates Figure 1 with explicit interaction-allocation and conflict diagrams. It adds Tables 1–5, Go visualizations in Figures 2–3, and image-coalition displays in Figures 4–7. These substantially expand the visual presentation beyond v2's single schematic.

improvement.justification: v3 makes coalition faithfulness operationally assessable and adds controlled synthetic validation plus concrete NLP, image and Go evidence, substantially improving the practical grounding of v2's theoretical proposal. Additional derivations and clearer organization also make the arguments easier to inspect. Real-world validation remains largely example-based, without uncertainty estimates or complete training details, but the gains in testability and supporting evidence are substantial.
